sections.1.0:
Welcome to the Bitcoin Diploma. Over the next ten weeks you'll build up an understanding of money — what it actually is, why it works the way it does, and where Bitcoin fits into that story.

This course is structured deliberately. Chapters 1 through 5 are entirely about money — its history, its properties, and the ways it can go wrong. Only in Chapter 6 do we actually arrive at Bitcoin itself. That's not padding. Everything you learn about money in the first half becomes the lens you'll use to evaluate Bitcoin in the second half.

Before we touch Bitcoin at all, we need to answer a much older question: why does money exist in the first place? It's tempting to skip straight to Bitcoin — it's the exciting part, after all — but doing that would be like trying to understand why a car's engine matters without first understanding why humans wanted to travel faster than walking.

If you get stuck on anything along the way, talk to Sassa — that's what the sessions with her are for.
sections.1.1:
This section kicks things off with something personal. Think about your own life here in Ekasi — the taxi you took this morning, the airtime you bought, the money your family sends between each other. All of that runs on an assumption most people never question: that money works.

Before we define it properly, answer honestly, in your own words: what do you actually use money for, day to day?

Here's a thought experiment worth sitting with before you answer: imagine waking up tomorrow and every rand note, every coin, and every number in every bank account in the country simply vanished overnight — but everything else stayed exactly the same. The taxis still run, the shops still have stock, people still have the same skills and the same needs. What would happen in the first hour? The first day? The first week?

Most people's instinct is that chaos would follow almost immediately — and that instinct is worth trusting. It tells you something important: money isn't just a convenience sitting on top of a working economy. It's closer to the nervous system of that economy — the thing that lets millions of separate decisions by strangers who've never met coordinate with each other.
